summary: Describes state machines for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) peer and for several kinds of authenticators: stand-alone, backend, and full. The state machines show how EAP can be implemented in different deployments. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Think of a board game with clear rules for what happens after each move. This memo draws the rulebook, as a set of steps and turns, for how computers should handle a login conversation.

subtitle: How peers and servers orchestrate authentication exchanges.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) allows flexible authentication methods, but implementers need clear rules for how to orchestrate the conversation between peers and authenticators.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides detailed state machines for peers, authenticators, and backend servers. State machines describe which states each party can be in, what signals trigger transitions, and what happens when entering a state.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can now follow a precise blueprint to handle EAP authentication correctly, reducing bugs and improving interoperability across different systems.

facts.label: Peer states
facts.value: 13 states from DISABLED to SUCCESS or FAILURE

today: RFC 4137 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard reference for implementing EAP state machines across peers, authenticators, and AAA servers.

sections.title: The EAP Switch Model
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) lets different authentication methods plug into a common conversation framework. At each end, a component called the EAP Switch sits between the EAP methods and the lower layer (such as PPP or 802.1X). The peer switch negotiates with the authenticator switch to choose which method to use, then steps aside to let the method do its work.

This RFC describes what happens inside the switch: how it waits for requests, how it routes packets to methods, how it handles retransmits, and how it knows when to stop. The model covers three real-world scenarios: a peer talking to a local authenticator, an authenticator talking to a backend server through pass-through, and a combined authenticator that can do both.
sections.eli5: The EAP Switch is like a receptionist: it answers the phone, figures out which department to transfer the call to, and keeps the call on track until it is done.

sections.title: State Machines and Transitions
sections.content:
A state machine has a set of states (like IDLE, RECEIVED, METHOD) and rules that say which states you can move to and when. Only one state is active at a time. Transitions happen when a condition is met, such as receiving a packet or reaching a timeout. On entry to a state, the machine runs procedures: it might parse an incoming packet, call a method, build a response, or signal the lower layer.

Variables track state: booleans flag whether a request was received, integers count retransmits, and enumerations track the current method state (CONT, MAY_CONT, DONE). The state machine reads these variables to decide which transition to take next.
sections.eli5: The state machine is like a flowchart where each box (state) has a list of things to do, and arrows show where to go next based on what just happened.

sections.title: How Peers Authenticate
sections.content:
The peer state machine receives requests from an authenticator and sends responses. It starts in DISABLED, moves to INITIALIZE when the port becomes available, then sits in IDLE waiting for requests. When a request arrives, it goes to RECEIVED to parse the packet. If the request asks for identity, the peer goes to IDENTITY state; if it asks for a specific method, the peer goes to GET_METHOD or METHOD. After the method processes the packet, the peer goes to SEND_RESPONSE to signal that a response is ready.

The peer tracks decision and methodState to know when to succeed or fail. If the method sets methodState to DONE and decision to UNCOND_SUCC (unconditionally successful), the peer waits for an EAP Success packet. If it gets EAP Failure instead, it moves to the FAILURE state, which is final. EAP Success moves the peer to the SUCCESS state, also final.
sections.eli5: The peer waits for homework questions (requests), answers them using the right tool (method), and sends back the homework (response). When the teacher says 'You passed' (EAP Success) or 'You failed' (EAP Failure), the homework is done.

sections.title: Authenticators: Local, Backend, and Full
sections.content:
An authenticator sits on the server side. The simplest is the stand-alone authenticator: it proposes an EAP method, processes peer responses, and decides success or failure on its own. It moves through states like IDLE, RECEIVED, PROPOSE_METHOD (choosing which method to try next), METHOD_REQUEST (building a request), METHOD_RESPONSE (processing the response), SELECT_ACTION (deciding if policy is satisfied), and finally SUCCESS or FAILURE.

A backend authenticator is used when the authenticator is just a relay: it forwards requests to an AAA server (such as RADIUS) that holds the actual methods. It has an extra state, PICK_UP_METHOD, to handle methods started by a pass-through authenticator. The full authenticator combines both: it can do local methods itself, or switch to pass-through mode to delegate to a backend.
sections.eli5: A stand-alone authenticator grades the homework itself. A backend authenticator is like a teaching assistant who sends the homework to the teacher to grade. A full authenticator can do both: grade simple problems itself or send harder ones to the teacher.

sections.title: Denial-of-Service Risks
sections.content:
Because EAP packets like Identity and Failure are not cryptographically protected, an attacker can inject or modify them. The RFC documents specific denial-of-service attacks that exploit the state machine: an attacker can send an EAP Failure before any method starts, forcing the peer to fail; or send endless Identity requests, preventing the peer from starting a real method. On the authenticator side, a fake NAK (negative acknowledgement) after the authenticator proposes a method can force it to try a different method.

The RFC recommends against trying to prevent these attacks by changing initial variable values, because doing so would break compatibility with legitimate peers or authenticators. Instead, the focus is on getting the state machine right so attackers cannot exploit implementation bugs. An accurate state machine reduces errors and thus reduces vulnerability.
sections.eli5: Without security, bad guys can send fake messages that fool either the peer or the authenticator into giving up or restarting when they should not. The state machine helps by being clear, so programmers do not make mistakes that give attackers an opening.

sections.title: Making State Machines Work
sections.content:
The RFC highlights implementation challenges: some state procedures may take a long time (asking the user for their identity, processing a method), and multithreaded implementations may need to run these in separate threads to avoid blocking the whole state machine. The RFC names specific vulnerable states (IDENTITY and METHOD_RESPONSE) where implementations should add timeouts so the machine can fail or retry if a procedure hangs.

Implementations are also free to add extra interfaces between methods and the lower layer beyond what this RFC defines. Interoperability note: some deployed authenticators generate EAP Success or Failure packets with the wrong Identifier field. The RFC documents a workaround (accepting either the matching ID or ID+1) but notes it is not recommended because it does not conform to RFC 3748.
sections.eli5: Real code has to handle slow operations (like waiting for a user to type) and buggy old servers. The state machine sets the rules, but each implementer has to decide how to handle delays and oddities in practice.
